Cyclone Arnab: Red alert in Odisha, Andhra Pradesh braces for landfall on October 28
Cyclone Arnab is gathering strength over the Bay of Bengal, putting Odisha and Andhra Pradesh on alert as authorities race to prepare for heavy rain and powerful winds. The India Meteorological Department (IMD) expects the storm to intensify into a very severe cyclonic storm before crossing the Andhra Pradesh coast near Yanam on the forenoon of October 28.
Odisha has mobilised 225 fire-service teams, more than 100 boats and specialised rescue equipment. The IMD has issued red and orange alerts for parts of the state, warning of extremely heavy rainfall in vulnerable districts. Schools, colleges and Anganwadi centres in affected districts are also reportedly being shut on October 28 and 29.
Cyclone Arnab: When and where will the storm make landfall?
The IMD said on October 26 that Cyclone Arnab was moving westwards over the east-central and adjoining west-central Bay of Bengal. It is forecast to intensify into a severe cyclonic storm by midnight on October 26 and a very severe cyclonic storm on October 27. The storm is expected to cross the Andhra Pradesh coast between Bapatla and Visakhapatnam, close to Yanam, with sustained wind speeds of 115-125 kmph and gusts reaching 140 kmph.
"It has intensified into cyclonic storm 'Arnab' today morning. By noon today, it is located over the central part of the Bay of Bengal, about 650 kilometres away from Kakinada," IMD Director General Mrutyunjay Mohapatra said.
He warned that sea conditions would deteriorate sharply, with wave heights potentially exceeding 14 metres on October 27. A storm surge of 1 to 1.5 metres above the astronomical tide could inundate low-lying areas along parts of the Andhra Pradesh coast.
Which Odisha districts face red and orange alerts?
Rainfall associated with the cyclone is expected to reach Odisha from the evening or night of October 27. The IMD has forecast heavy to very heavy rainfall in districts including Puri, Ganjam, Gajapati, Rayagada and Koraput on October 27.
On October 28, isolated extremely heavy rainfall is likely in Ganjam, Gajapati, Rayagada, Koraput and Malkangiri. Heavy rainfall could also affect parts of western and coastal Odisha, raising concerns about flooding and landslides.
The IMD expects rainfall activity to continue into October 29, easing substantially from October 30. Authorities have urged fishermen not to venture into the sea and warned that railways, roads, flights, ports and shipping could face disruption.
How is Odisha preparing for Cyclone Arnab?
Odisha’s Fire and Emergency Services has identified Malkangiri, Koraput, Rayagada, Nabarangpur, Gajapati and Ganjam as priority districts. Inspector General of Police Umashankar Dash told ANI that 225 teams were being deployed, supported by more than 100 boats and a round-the-clock state command centre.
The National Disaster Response Force has deployed five teams in Odisha, mobilised four for Visakhapatnam and deployed another four for Chhattisgarh, according to NDRF officer Santosh Kumar Paswan, who spoke to ANI.
The Cabinet Secretariat said on October 26 that the National Crisis Management Committee had reviewed preparedness for the approaching cyclone. Authorities are coordinating rescue operations and monitoring vulnerable areas as the storm advances.
With landfall expected on October 28, officials are urging residents in vulnerable areas to follow local advisories, avoid the sea and prepare for possible evacuation. The cyclone’s precise impacts will depend on its track and intensity over the next two days.
(With inputs from ANI)

title: Cyclone Arnab: Where It Is Heading, When It Could Make Landfall And Why It Has This Name - Brut
full_text:
Cyclone Arnab is approaching India's eastern coast, putting Andhra Pradesh and Odisha on alert ahead of its expected landfall on Wednesday, 28 October. As authorities prepare for the approaching storm, questions are emerging about its potential impact, evacuation plans and the measures being taken to protect vulnerable communities.
But why is this cyclone called Arnab? Who named Cyclone Arnab, how are cyclone names selected, and why do storms around the world get distinct names?

Where Is Cyclone Arnab Heading?
Cyclone Arnab formed over the Bay of Bengal and intensified into a cyclonic storm. According to the India Meteorological Department's (IMD) forecast on 26 October, the storm is moving towards the Andhra Pradesh coast and could cross the coastline between Bapatla and Visakhapatnam by the forenoon of 28 October.
The IMD has forecast that the system could intensify into a very severe cyclonic storm before landfall. Maximum sustained wind speeds are expected to reach 115–125 kmph, with gusts of up to 140 kmph.
Northern and central coastal districts of Andhra Pradesh are expected to experience heavy to extremely heavy rainfall. Southern parts of Odisha could also face intense rain, making preparations necessary beyond the area where the cyclone is expected to make landfall.
The storm's track and intensity may change as the system develops. Residents in potentially affected areas should follow official weather bulletins and advisories issued by local authorities.

From Evacuations To Emergency Teams: What Measures Are Being Taken?
Authorities in Andhra Pradesh and Odisha are preparing for the possibility of flooding, power cuts and damage to homes and infrastructure as Cyclone Arnab approaches the coast.
In Andhra Pradesh, Chief Minister N Chandrababu Naidu has directed district administrations to remain on high alert, set up control rooms and send regular updates to residents' mobile phones. Officials have also been asked to arrange the safe evacuation of people from vulnerable coastal villages.
The state has identified approximately 5.7 lakh people living in vulnerable areas who may need to be evacuated. Authorities said evacuations were scheduled to begin on Monday evening, 26 October. Authorities have instructed boats at sea to return to shore and asked electricity officials to prepare for the speedy restoration of power following any disruption.
Andhra Pradesh Home Minister Vangalapudi Anitha has directed officials to remove dangerous hoardings, keep National Disaster Response Force (NDRF) and State Disaster Response Force (SDRF) teams ready, and ensure that rescue operations can begin without delay.
Officials have also been asked to restrict access to beaches in affected areas. Fishermen have been advised against venturing into the sea, while residents have been warned against approaching rough waters.
“Odisha, meanwhile, is preparing to relocate people from low-lying areas to cyclone shelters. Schools and colleges in five districts, Ganjam, Gajapati, Rayagada, Koraput and Malkangiri, are scheduled to close on Wednesday and Thursday, 28 and 29 October, as a precaution.”
At the national level, Cabinet Secretary TV Somanathan chaired a meeting of the National Crisis Management Committee on 26 October to review preparations. Central and state agencies are coordinating their response, with the focus on preventing casualties and restoring essential services quickly.

Why Are Cyclones Given Names?
A cyclone's name is more than a label. It helps meteorologists, emergency services, governments and the public identify a particular storm throughout its development.
When several weather systems are being tracked across the ocean, referring to each one only by its location or technical description can make warnings harder to follow. A distinct name makes official alerts easier to communicate, remember and share.
Naming also reduces confusion when several cyclones develop in the same region or when a storm's forecast changes.
The World Meteorological Organization (WMO) and the United Nations Economic and Social Commission for Asia and the Pacific (UNESCAP) oversee the regional naming arrangement through their Panel on Tropical Cyclones. The system for the North Indian Ocean began in September 2004.
Not every weather disturbance receives a name immediately. The Regional Specialised Meteorological Centre in New Delhi, operated by the IMD, assigns names to qualifying tropical cyclones over the Bay of Bengal and the Arabian Sea once they reach the required intensity.

Why Is The Cyclone Called Arnab?
The name Arnab was proposed by Bangladesh. It appears in the official list of tropical cyclone names adopted in April 2020 by the WMO/ESCAP Panel on Tropical Cyclones.
The official list gives the prescribed pronunciation as “Ornab”. The name is commonly associated with the Bengali word for the ocean or sea, although the official naming list does not provide a formal definition.
However, the cyclone's name does not indicate which country it will hit. Bangladesh proposed the name, but the storm is approaching India's eastern coast. The naming system operates regionally, with names drawn from a pre-approved list rather than chosen according to the country where a storm is expected to make landfall.

How Does The Cyclone Naming System Work?
The current North Indian Ocean naming list includes contributions from 13 countries: Bangladesh, India, Iran, the Maldives, Myanmar, Oman, Pakistan, Qatar, Saudi Arabia, Sri Lanka, Thailand, the United Arab Emirates and Yemen.
Each country submitted 13 names, creating a list of 169 names. The names are arranged by country and used sequentially, column by column, as qualifying cyclones develop.
The list includes names such as Gati, Tej, Remal and Dana, alongside Arnab. Once a name from this regional list has been used, it is not used again under the system's rules.
The names are therefore selected well in advance. They are not chosen in response to a cyclone's strength, its expected path or the place where it eventually makes landfall.
This also means that India does not name every cyclone that approaches its coast. The IMD assigns names from the shared list when the relevant criteria are met.
